correctness.rationale: For input ones at i<j the one-deletion outputs of weight one have their one at i or j−1. They coincide exactly for adjacent ones. Thus if L selected words have adjacent ones and S do not, L+2S≤n−1. Consecutive starts for the adjacent words collide on a weight-two output, so L≤ceil((n−1)/2); taking floors gives the claimed upper bound. In the construction adjacent starts are even and spaced by two while the gap-three starts are 1 mod 4. The weight-one outputs are disjoint (one even index per adjacent word or a disjoint pair of odd indices for each gap-three word). For weight-two outputs the new first-one positions for distinct starts within either family lie in disjoint sets {i−1,i}, with unavailable positions at the boundary simply excluded. Across families the output gap is one versus two or three, so the descendants are disjoint. Counting the two families saturates the bound, including the sole word at n=2.
